messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Potter
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 50

# The Weight of Clay

Harjit is a seventy-five-year-old man who came to this country as a refugee more than four decades ago, fleeing the communal violence that consumed his village in the Punjab during a period of brutal political upheaval. He arrived with almost nothing — his wife Amrita, a small cloth bundle, and the particular silence of a man who has witnessed things he cannot yet name. He has been married to Amrita for fifty-two years, and she remains, by his own account, the primary reason he gets out of bed each morning.

What Harjit lost in those weeks of flight was not only his home. He watched his younger brother shot in a roadway. He spent three nights hiding in a drainage ditch with Amrita and two other families, listening to sounds he has never described in full to anyone, including his children. He crossed two borders on foot, was detained briefly at a checkpoint where soldiers struck him across the shoulders with a rifle stock, and finally arrived at a processing camp where he waited for seven months in conditions he describes only as "not fit for animals." He does not speak of these events in sequence. He speaks of them the way a man speaks of weather — in fragments, sideways, as though looking directly at them might cause him to go blind.

For many years, Harjit managed. He established himself as a potter, a craft he had learned from his father, and built a small studio behind his house where he has worked every day for thirty years. The rhythm of the wheel, the pressure of his hands on wet clay, gave him a structure that kept the worst of it at bay. His children grew up watching him work. He was present, mostly. He provided. He prayed.

But in the last two years, since his retirement from the small teaching studio he ran at a local arts centre, the structure has collapsed. Without the fixed hours, without students who needed him to be steady, Harjit finds the days formless and dangerous. He sits in his studio but cannot always bring himself to touch the clay. When he does work, he sometimes stops abruptly and stands at the window for long stretches, watching the garden with an expression Amrita describes as "gone away somewhere I cannot follow."

He sleeps poorly and wakes between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering, certain — for a few terrible seconds — that he is back in the ditch, or on the road, or at the checkpoint. He does not always know where he is when he first opens his eyes. He has begun sleeping on his side of the bed closest to the door, something Amrita noticed before he did. He does not watch the news. He cannot tolerate the sound of shouting, even from a television in another room. Last spring, a car backfired on his street and he found himself crouched behind the garden wall, shaking, before he understood what had happened.

He tells these things carefully, with a kind of dignified precision, as though precision might contain them. He is a proud man who raised three children, built something from nothing, and has always understood hard work as the appropriate response to suffering. Asking for help sits uncomfortably with him, and he frames his attendance here as something his GP "insisted upon," though he admits, quietly, that he has been frightened by what is happening to his mind.

What troubles him most, he says, is not the nightmares or the startling. It is the sense that the past has become more vivid than the present — that his brother's face, which he has not been able to picture clearly for forty years, now appears to him constantly, young and unaware of what is coming. Harjit keeps returning to the clay as a kind of answer to this, shaping and reshaping the same bowl, as though the right form might eventually hold everything he cannot say.
